translation: The most important event for me during the winter of 1993 was my father's return, just one week before my mother's wedding.
One December afternoon, he came to find me at school.
I rushed out towards the front gate and saw him from distance through the iron bars, standing outside smoking a cigarette.
He was wearing a long black trench coat with its collar up that covered half of his face.
For some reason I couldn't even see his face clearly but it already felt like he had been going through some tough times .
My heart sunk and tears streamed down my cheeks.
I never thought that my mother would contemplate remarrying.
Maybe subconsciously, I believed she should continue to suffer because of my father's departure, just like me.
Moreover, I felt she lacked the ability to find happiness.
Perhaps this was indeed the case, but happiness had the ability to find her.
Isn't it so?
For a beautiful woman, there is no need for such struggles; she doesn't have to do anything but simply stand still.
I still remember, the winter of that year was particularly long, half of April had passed and the winter jasmine still hadn't bloomed.
The divorce of your parents put you in a very depressed mood.
We haven't had any new games for a long time, and when evening comes, we would sit idly on the roof of the dead man's tower.
Among the scattered body parts in our courtyard, few more arms were added.
We used hooks to gather them together and arranged them into a thousand-armed Guanyin statue.
In fact, my father had no idea how to do business.
He had just gone to throw in his lot with a cousin whom he didn't know very well.
My grandmother had a younger sister who went to Beijing many years ago and later got married and had children there.
This older cousin was her eldest son, who had always been an oddity in our entire family.
You just said that everyone has a time when their fate begins, as if life is suddenly reined in.
Mine must have been at the age of eight.
That autumn, my father left Jinan and went to Beijing alone.
Since then, I have never had a home again.
I had no intend to keep the appointment.
Regardless of the reason, I believe there is no longer a need for us to meet again.
I sat on the sofa, smoking cigarette after cigarette, as it got darker and darker outside.
Suddenly, there was a knock at the door.
The water delivery boy stood in the doorway carrying buckets of water, saying he was delivering water to a household in the western suburbs.
He was wearing a dirty grey knit hat and looked dazed.
Our conversation was a struggle.
Each time we fell into silence, I felt a pressure on my heart and all I wanted was to end this meeting quickly.
You seemed to notice but were still trying hard to find something to talk about.
As the tea got cold and the white fog in the room had cleared completely, you finally stood up to leave.
Just after I closed the door, heaving a sigh of relief, the doorbell rang again; you were standing at my doorstep inviting me over for an evening at Xiaobai Building.
Before I could even decline your invitation, you had already walked out from under my apartment building's archway.
I walked into the kitchen and turned off the stove.
Half of the water had already evaporated, and the whole room was shrouded in white mist.
You sat down nervously, watching me pour tea.
"Do you still live with your grandmother and aunt?" you asked.
I told you that my grandmother had passed away, so now it's only me and my aunt living together.
"She never married," you asked.
"Yes.
The haze of breath you exhaled, the tendrils of hair stirred by the wind, and your slightly trembling knees under your coat all these convinced me that you were indeed standing before me.
Not an extension of my previous dream.
After eighteen years apart not recognizing each other is to be expected.
You were not disguised with makeup; your pale face was a bit swollen, but at least it didn't betray everyone's expectations; you've grown into a beauty.
Only that petite cheek of yours displayed a grim expression, like someone who has stayed in a big city for too long.
You asked if you appeared different from what I imagined.
I just laughed without giving an answer.
To be honest, I never actually envisioned what you would look like as an adult.

Everything related to you had already been filed away and sealed off with wax in my memory vaults long ago—a tad harsh words to say maybe—however truthfully speaking, I really hadn't anticipated seeing you again.
I opened my eyes.
You were standing in the doorway.
I didn't know how long you had been standing there, for all I knew, you might have even seen me laughing in my sleep.
Or the sadness of waking up, or what I look like at my weakest moments.
Cheng
Gong, you called out my name in a low voice--your voice was very hoarse as though it had been a long time since you last spoke.
It was about to snow—the sky looked terribly overcast and the room was pitch dark.
The water on the stove boiled rapidly with a gurgling noise that filled the room.
I looked at you carefully for a moment to make sure that I did not recognize you.

But under the dim light, I suddenly felt this stranger standing opposite me seemed to have deep connection with my life—an eerie feeling which sent shivers down my spine briefly—I worked hard to rethink; flipping through memory cards in mind like rapid shots of an old film strip reveal scenes from past—Suddenly then –you spoke out: "You are Li Jiaqi".
